title: Conditionals, Question Forms, and Negation
shortDescription: If-clauses that decide real vs imaginary outcomes, plus the question-tag and double-negative traps that sneak into error-spotting.
genZNote: Conditionals are English's 'what if' machine — swap one tense and you flip a sentence from likely to purely hypothetical.

rows: General truth/fact: If you heat water, it boils.
Real, likely future possibility: If it rains, I will stay home.
Unreal/hypothetical present or future: If I were rich, I would travel the world.
Unreal past — something that didn't happen: If I had studied, I would have passed.

sections.heading: Conditional exam traps
bullets: In Second Conditional, use 'WERE' for all subjects (I, he, she, it), not 'was' — 'If I WERE you...' is the traditional correct/formal form, though 'was' is common informally.
Never use 'will' inside the if-clause itself: 'If it will rain' is wrong; it should be 'If it rains.'
Third Conditional talks about a past that CANNOT be changed — mixing tenses (e.g., 'If I had studied, I would pass' instead of 'would have passed') is a frequent error.
Mixed conditionals exist (a past condition with a present result, or vice versa) but are less commonly tested at this level than the four standard types.

sections.heading: Question formation basics
bullets: Yes/No questions invert the subject and the auxiliary/modal verb: 'She IS coming' → 'IS she coming?'; if there's no auxiliary, add 'do/does/did': 'She likes tea' → 'Does she like tea?'
Wh-questions (what, where, when, why, who, how) go: Wh-word + auxiliary + subject + main verb: 'Where IS she going?'
When 'who'/'what' IS the subject of the question, no auxiliary inversion is needed: 'WHO called you?' (not 'Who did call you?').

sections.heading: Question tags — the pattern that trips people up
bullets: A positive statement takes a NEGATIVE tag, and vice versa: 'She is coming, ISN'T she?' / 'He doesn't like tea, DOES he?'
The tag's auxiliary must match the main sentence's tense/auxiliary: 'They have finished, HAVEN'T they?'
After 'let's', the tag is always 'shall we': 'Let's go, SHALL we?'
After an imperative, the tag is usually 'will you': 'Close the door, WILL you?'

sections.heading: Negation and the double-negative trap
bullets: Standard English avoids double negatives: 'I don't have no money' is non-standard; it should be 'I don't have ANY money' or 'I have NO money.'

Words like 'hardly', 'scarcely', 'barely', 'never', 'no one' are already negative — pairing them with another negative word creates an unintended double negative: 'I can't hardly see' should be 'I can HARDLY see' or 'I CAN'T see.'
'Neither' pairs with 'nor', not 'or', to keep the negative sense consistent across a sentence.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Conditionals (zero, first, second, third) use different tense pairings to show fact, likely possibility, unreal present, or unreal past; question forms and negation have their own agreement and inversion rules.
keyFacts: Second Conditional traditionally uses 'were' for all subjects.
A positive statement takes a negative question tag, and vice versa.
Words like hardly/scarcely/barely are already negative — don't double them up.

highYieldFacts: Third Conditional = had + V3 in the if-clause, would have + V3 in the main clause — for an unchangeable past.
'I can't hardly wait' is a double negative error; correct is 'I can hardly wait.'
commonTraps: Mismatched question tags (positive statement + positive tag).
mustRemember: Match the conditional type to the intended reality: possible future (first), unreal now (second), unreal past (third).

confusedTerms.distinction: Second Conditional imagines an unreal PRESENT/future ('If I were rich, I would travel'). Third Conditional imagines an unreal PAST that already happened differently ('If I had been rich, I would have travelled').

possibleQuestions: Spot the error: 'If I will have time, I will visit you.'
Add the correct question tag: 'You haven't finished your homework, ___?'
